title: On-chip Radio Frequency Maser
authors: Hongliang Wu, Zhengtao Wang, Yuchen Han, Liu Yang, Zhiwei Wang, Yeliang Wang, Dezhi Zheng, Bo Zhang, Jun Zhang
abstract: Room-temperature solid-state masers offer exceptional frequency selectivity and ultra-low noise for weak-signal detection. However, their reliance on bulky metallic resonators has significantly hindered integration, miniaturization, and extension to lower frequencies. Here, we demonstrate the first on-chip radio-frequency maser operating at room temperature, exploiting optically pumped triplet states of pentacene. The device produces stimulated emission at 106.62 MHz and enables ultra-sensitive microwave magnetic-field detection with a sensitivity of ($\sim 10\,\rm{fT/\sqrt{Hz}}$), functioning simultaneously as a local oscillator and a sensor. By actively controlling microwave dissipation, we achieve efficient regulation of the maser output, revealing a key mechanism for tuning emission in open cavity-free systems. This work extends pentacene-based masers into the radio-frequency regime and establishes a highly integrated on-chip architecture for room-temperature masers, offering a new pathway toward portable quantum devices.
summary: The research presents the first on-chip radio-frequency maser using optically pumped pentacene at room temperature. By integrating the gain medium into a compact LC resonator and implementing active feedback control over the circuit's quality factor, the authors achieved stable microwave emission and demonstrated ultra-sensitive magnetic field detection ($\sim 10 	ext{ fT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$). This establishes a highly integrated platform for portable quantum sensing.
main_problem: To develop a highly integrated, room-temperature solid-state maser operating at radio frequencies (RF) for applications like ultra-sensitive microwave magnetic-field detection.
main_result: The authors demonstrated the first on-chip RF maser using pentacene, achieving stimulated emission at 106.62 MHz and reaching a magnetic-field sensitivity of $\sim 10 	ext{ fT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$.
method: They utilized an optically pumped system within a compact on-chip LC resonant circuit, employing active feedback control to tune the resonator's quality factor ($Q_L$) between oscillator and sensing regimes.
model_or_system: The physical platform is pentacene doped p-terphenyl exhibiting optically pumped triplet states ($T_1$). The maser operates by exploiting the X-Y sublevel transition ($\sim 106$ MHz) within an LC resonator structure integrated on a chip, replacing bulky metallic resonators.
key_observables: Maser output signal intensity (showing $\propto \sqrt{E_{	ext{pump}}}$ dependence), stable oscillation spectra locked to the X-Y frequency, and magnetic field response ($\partial S / \partial B_1$).
important_parameters: Operating frequency of 106.62 MHz; sensitivity of $10 	ext{ fT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$; tunability via controlling $Q_L$ from intrinsic ($\approx 40$) to several thousand.
main_assumptions: The threshold pump energy required for low-$Q_L$ operation far exceeds the pentacene damage threshold, suggesting improving the intrinsic $Q_L$ is necessary for further development.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanism (pumping $ightarrow T_1 ightarrow X-Y$ inversion) and the two operating regimes. Time-domain data shows signal build-up, FFT confirms stable oscillation, and plots demonstrate intensity scaling with pump energy and threshold dependence on $Q_L$.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical mechanism of optical pumping in pentacene to achieve triplet state inversion, describes the integration into an LC resonator circuit, presents experimental results showing tunable operation between maser oscillation (high $Q_L$) and sensitive sensing (low $Q_L$), and concludes with performance metrics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses solid-state quantum emitters for microwave detection. The ability to integrate the gain medium into a chip-scale resonator while actively tuning its coupling strength ($Q_L$) is highly relevant for building portable, high-performance quantum sensors that bridge fundamental physics with practical engineering.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The mechanism of LF maser. (a) Pentacene molecules are pumped by a 590-nm pulse, followed by ISC and rapid IC to the first triplet excited state T1. In the ab- sence of an external magnetic field, the T1 state spontaneously splits into the X, Y, and Z sublevels. The population ratio between the X and Y sublevels is approximately 0.76: 0.16. X-Y inversion drives the approximately 106-MHz transition. (b) High QL supports self-oscillation while low QL suppresses oscillation and enables magnetic-field sensing.

FIG. 2. Setup for the LF maser. A gain-adjustable feedback loop tunes the LC circuit QL and switches between oscillator and sensing regimes. A logarithmic detector can be added at the position marked by a red star to convert the time-domain signal into an envelope signal.

FIG. 4. The sensitivity of the magnetic-field sensing. The green points represent the signal strengths measured at different microwave magnetic fields and are fitted by an ex- ponential equation. The slope at each data point can be ob- tained from the fitted curve, which is the responsivity of the system to the magnetic field.

FIG. 3. Performance of the microwave quantum os- cillator. (a) The upper panel shows the time-domain data of LF maser pulses. The lower panel provides a detailed view of the position of maximum maser output. The dots represent the data points acquired by the oscilloscope, and the solid line is the sinusoidal fit. (b) Emission spectra of the LF maser. Emission remains centered at 106.62 MHz over repeated tri- als. (c) The maser output peak intensity versus the pump energy under different QL. The relationship clearly follows a square-root function. (d) Linear relationship between the Q−1 L and the threshold pump energy. The threshold is defined at 1 µW maser output.

Spintronics.note: The research describes an optically pumped solid-state maser utilizing triplet states ($T_1$) in a semiconductor (pentacene) integrated with an LC resonator, which directly falls under the scope of coupling quantum optics concepts to magnetic/spin systems.

Magnetic noise spectroscopy.note: The central result is achieving ultra-sensitive magnetic field detection ($\sim 10 	ext{ fT}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$) via a resonant cavity system, which directly relates to the goal of developing or applying theory for measuring magnetic noise near a probe.
